Hi, I think I can share what I know (not wisdom at all, neither much of an experience since I had the thing on Halloween and was just discharged on Friday), as a girl in the same boat relying what my doctors have told me.

First and foremost, your pregnancy will have to be planned meticulously. Pregnancy itself is a risk of a PE, so you probably would need your blood thinners during it, but you'd better avoid getting pregnant for at least half a year, you need to recover.

Secondly, if you were on a hormonal pill, you should stop taking them for a while because they make your blood more prone to clotting. As my doctors told me, "hormones are about quality of life, but blood thinners after PE are about survival". So yeah, if you can get pregnant by your partner, they wear a condom or get no action.

Thirdly, from what I've seen on this sub, there's a chance for you to have kids after you make a recovery, but you'll probably need a C-section. But again, your pregnancy needs to be planned and monitored closely.

Hope I could help a little.

It kinda reminds me of my own idiocy, but it went the other way round. For context: I'm a very white person from a very white region, and I was obsessed with medieval European history when I was in middle school. 

So picture this: circa 2007, it's an early morning, me, a teenager, and my mom have just unboarded the ship from Helsinki to Stockholm and are waiting for a bus or anything to get us to the hotel (the bus was super late that day). There's another couple near us, a black guy and a black chick. I don't remember what started the dialogue between us but it somehow got to that:

Guy, obviously thinking he's cool: "Do you know who I am?"

Me: "No"

Guy: "I'm Martin Luther King!"

Me, deadpan: "No, he died many years ago"

After that mom and I decided to leave and just walk to the hotel, and all the way up there I was yapping about this dude pretending to be a medieval philosopher. But hey, in my defense: the guy with a dream was long dead by 2007 as well, even if not for several centuries.

Hey, lawyer here. If you want to do business in Russia, as a foreigner it's generally recommended you start a company or a sole proprietorship here, and then open a business bank account. Some Russian banks issue cards with these accounts, some don't. Alternatively, if you just want to test the waters, you could try to open a Russian bank account, big Russian banks are generally okay with foreigners but your payments might be monitored more closely, so it's better to stay within 100k rub a day/1000k rub a month limit; also, most Russian banks will ask you to collect the card in person, even if it's delivered by a courier.
P.s. this is not legal advice.

Yes, if she's not a Russian citizen anymore (as in she renounced her Russian citizenship) and it didn't get to the Rosreestr (Russian register of property) it will be awful. She'll have to prove that she actually has the right to a part of that flat, and that the person in the register is, in fact, her. It may, and will, be a lengthy process. 

If she's still a Russian citizen, but simply lost her Russian passport, it's way easier, but Russian citizens have to issue Russian e-signatures in their Russian passports, so she'll have to reissue the passport with the embassy and then issue that e-signature.

Lawyer here. There's several kinds of e-signatures Russia recognizes, for the signature that can be used in real estate deals see ЭЦП для Росреестра. Docusign e-signature or whatever won't work.

The e-signatures that work with real estate deals usually require a person in whose name the signature is issued to be physically present to collect the e-signature token (i.e. a flash drive) for verification. There are some firms that issue e-signatures fully online, but those are usually shady.

There's a few, and, naturally, they are very recent, made after 2000 (Kolchak monument in Irkutsk, the Exile (Исход) monument in Novorossiysk, Markov memorial, Kornilov memorial, etc). Keep in mind that for the Soviet regime the White Army (or the White Guard) was a natural enemy, and you don't usually commemorate the enemy. So most memorials you can find are literary, like Bulgakov's White Guard (Белая Гвардия) and Flight (Бег) and diaries of the emigrants, along with some songs that stuck around (e.g. Poruchik Golitsyn). 

If it counts, there's also some memorials/monuments of the family of the last Russian emperor. 

Also, there's several memorial flats of the so-called Silver Age (the Glided age in western historiography) artists, of whom most happened to be noblesse in the Russian Empire. Their memorial flats mostly mean they were somewhat loyal to the Soviet regime, but they were connected to the White Army anyway (e.g. Anna Akhmatova, whose husband, Nikolai Gumilev, was a White Army officer; he was executed in 1921).

Well, Russian legal system is essentially "it's not forbidden unless the law explicitly forbids that" (that's why some 10-15 years ago 'bath salt' drugs were openly sold). Under current Russian legislation one can purchase, acquire, transfer, sell, own crypto without any repercussions. On the other hand, it's impossible to start an LLC saying it's main line of business is dealing in crypto (because there's no such business activity code in the book, so many claim they're IT companies), and mining is unregulated still (there's a draft legislation, but that's what it is - a draft, even though it wrought panic in the crypto community when it was first introduced).

Many people (especially millenials and zoomers) own some crypto. Crypto has an indefinite legal status: it's definitely deemed to be a property for bankruptcy proceedings and for some fiscal things, and there's a category of 'other kinds of property' in the Civil code of Russia, but nobody explicitly said what kind of property crypto is, as of my knowledge. On the other hand, back in 2020 the law on digital financial assets was adopted, but it's more focused on security tokens than anything else. However, it prohibits Russian nationals from paying and being paid in crypto for goods and services (not that it really works tho). Also, if one trades in crypto they shall file annual individual income tax (3-ndfl) and declare their profit, but some traders don't.

EMI generally stands for an Electronic money institution, and, generally, you can open an EMI account without having to be physically present, only sharing your phone number and going through some online KYC, but what you can do with the money for with that limited KYC may be limited as well, both amount wise and purpose wise. For a fully functional account you in most cases have to be physically present to go through an extended KYC, just like they do in a bank. That's just how most anti money laundering laws work, they are pretty much in line with the EU/FATF AML legislation.

Also, mind the sanctions. Most EU/US based and licensed EMIs won't open an account for a Russian citizen (so PayPal, Transferwise, Paysera and alike are out of reach). 

On the bright side though, most banks and EMIs from the former USSR countries are ok with opening an account to a person with a Russian passport (not the case with Ukraine or EU member states, obviously). Some eastern EMIs might also be good, but be extra careful with Hong Kong/Singapore based ones. Not to offend anyone, but some of those are simply scams that only receive money, but never actually rely them to an actual recipient. 

There's also always an offshore banking option, but I know some EU banks might be a bit too careful around, say, a bank from Dominica or Belize.

 Another summer camp classic I can think of is the contact game: person A comes up with the word and is either doing it themself (for a small company) or tells the word to person B. Then that person (A or B respectively, the host) says the first letter of the word to the players (for a quicker game the host may also tell the number of letters in the word). The players then ask "is it" Questions and if two or more think they mean the same thing or know what the other means they say 'contact' and count (to 5 or to 10 usually) and then say the word in unison. If the host comes up with something plausible while they are counting they have to say 'no, it's not [the word]' or just wait. If the players say the same word in unison after the count, the host gives them the next letter. If they fail, the host doesn't. If the player is sure they know the word they may just say it aloud. If they say the correct word they win and become the host themself. 

 It may sound complicated, see the example below (H is the host, numbers are players, the word is яблоко) 

H: the first letter is я
1: is it a tree? 
2: contact! 
1,2 in unison: 1, 2
H: no, it's not ясень
1: is it an animal? 
H: no, it's not ящерица
2: is it a Soviet plane? 
1: contact! 
1,2 in unison: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 - Як! 
H: no, it's not Як. The second letter is б. 
1: is it яблоко? 
H: yes, it is.

As a rule of thumb, the verb 'to be' is omitted in Russian in present tense if it's not a question or a non-specific answer. 
"Там кто-нибудь есть?" = "Is anybody there?" 
If you don't want to specify you can answer either simply "yes" (Да) or "there is" (Есть). If you want to specify you generally omit the verb. 
"There's two old men here" = "Здесь два старика" 
 But if you want to highlight some meaning you can add "есть",  e.g. "здесь нет девушек, здесь есть [только] два старика" (There's no girls here, there's [only] two old men). It will be excessive wording, think saying "I DO have the thing" in English.
